card.official_title: PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
card.plain_title: Make temporary income tax rates on high earners permanent
card.yes_means: The higher income tax rates paid by the top 2 percent of California taxpayers would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
card.no_means: The higher income tax rates would remain temporary and expire in 2031 under current law.

what_changes.today: The higher rates apply to the top 2 percent of taxpayers and expire in 2031.
what_changes.if_passes: Those existing higher rates would become permanent.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: The state Constitution sets a minimum funding level for schools and community colleges.
what_changes.if_passes: The analyst estimates roughly 40 percent of the measure's funding would go to schools and community colleges.
what_changes.label: prediction

what_changes.today: Income taxes fund health care and other services through the state's main operating account.
what_changes.if_passes: The analyst estimates the rest of the funding would go to other state programs, with part set aside in budget reserves.
what_changes.label: prediction

who_is_affected: High-income taxpayers who pay the temporary higher rates
K–12 students, families, and school staff
People who use Medi-Cal and other state-funded services

fiscal_impact.text: Compared with letting the higher rates expire in 2031, the measure would preserve $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state income tax revenue.
fiscal_impact.label: fact

steelman_yes.headline: This common-sense measure will definitely protect every classroom from devastating cuts, so voters should vote yes, as every reasonable Californian already knows.
more_reasons: Supporters argue continued revenue would also protect Medi-Cal and other health services.
Supporters argue local control, annual audits, and limits on administrative spending would protect classroom funds.

best_evidence.text: The analyst estimates roughly 40 percent of the measure's funding would go to schools and community colleges.
best_evidence.label: prediction

best_evidence.text: The official summary states that tax revenues are allocated 89 percent to K–12 schools and 11 percent to community colleges, with local school board spending decisions and no administrative costs.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_yes.who_it_helps: Supporters say students, school staff, and families relying on public health care would benefit.
steelman_yes.answer_to_other_side: Supporters argue keeping existing rates, rather than increasing them now, is worth preventing funding losses; they point to school spending safeguards.

steelman_no.headline: Opponents are wealthy people who don't want to pay their fair share; it's a power grab funded by special interests.

best_evidence.text: The measure would remove the scheduled 2031 expiration of the higher income tax rates.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_no.who_it_helps: Opponents say rejection would help affected taxpayers by keeping their scheduled tax relief.

crux.text: The choice weighs continued public-service funding against scheduled tax relief for high earners. The sides also disagree about whether spending reforms could protect services without extending the tax.

evidence.text: The measure keeps existing higher rates; it does not raise them above today's levels, but it prevents their scheduled expiration.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: The top 2 percent of taxpayers pay these higher rates and account for about half of all state income taxes.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: Annual revenue would vary widely because much of the taxed income is tied to the stock market; permanent rates do not mean a fixed yearly amount.
evidence.label: prediction

evidence.text: The official summary allocates tax revenues 89 percent to K–12 schools and 11 percent to community colleges, and says the measure increases General Fund revenues available for health care, reserves, and other programs.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: In its estimate of funding effects, the analyst says roughly 40 percent of funding would go to schools and community colleges, with the rest supporting other programs and reserves.
evidence.label: prediction
